levels.title: Words, lines and contested texts: reading at the smallest scale and arguing about poems

units.title: Reading at the smallest scale: one word, one line, one sound, one whole poem

lessons.title: The work one word does: ‘charter’d’ and ‘mark’ in Blake’s ‘London’
lessons.explanation: Close reading often begins with the largest units — plot, character, theme — and works downward. This lesson begins at the other end, with a single word, because in Blake’s ‘London’ the difference between two printings of the stanza’s third line changes the grammar of the whole stanza, and therefore changes who is doing what. The plate text, as transcribed on Wikisource under the 1826 copy of Songs of Innocence and of Experience, reads: ‘I wander thro’ each charter’d street, / Near where the charter’d Thames does flow, / And mark in every face I meet, / Marks of weakness, marks of woe.’ The 1901 letterpress edition on Project Gutenberg prints the same stanza as ‘I wander through each chartered street, / Near where the chartered Thames does flow, / A mark in every face I meet, / Marks of weakness, marks of woe.’ One word: ‘And mark’ against ‘A mark’. With ‘And mark’, the wandering speaker is the subject of his own act of reading: I wander and I mark, and the line’s object is what he finds — marks of weakness, marks of woe. With ‘A mark’, that verb disappears; ‘a mark in every face I meet’ is a noun phrase, and the next line’s plural ‘Marks’ has to carry the sentence as a verb, so the mark itself does the meaning-work: every face bears a mark, and the mark signifies weakness and woe. The reprint is therefore not merely modernising orthography. It withdraws the walker from the act of interpretation, in a poem whose last stanza has him hear a harlot’s curse that ‘Blasts the new born Infant’s tear’. Word-level choices also carry metre and personification: the plate’s apostrophes in ‘charter’d’, ‘thro’’, ‘mind-forg’d’ and ‘black’ning’ are printed instructions to elide, keeping the first three lines at eight syllables each and the fourth at seven, and the plate’s capitals in ‘every Man’, ‘the Chimney-sweeper’s cry’, ‘Church’, ‘Soldier’s’, ‘Harlot’s’ and ‘Marriage hearse’ treat those nouns as agents rather than as background scenery [1][2][3].
lessons.example: Work the argument as evidence rather than as preference. Three witnesses are available to anyone with a browser, and each one costs something. First, the Wikisource transcription of the plate under the 1826 copy gives ‘And mark in every face I meet’; the page itself carries a ‘no scan’ notice, so what you are reading is a transcription, not the engraved plate, and you should say so in any citation. Second, the Notebook draft of 1793, also transcribed on Wikisource, gives ‘And [see del.] mark in every face I meet’, where the transcriber marks an earlier word ‘see’ as deleted and ‘mark’ as surviving; it also shows the openings that were later replaced, ‘I wander thro’ each dirty street’ for ‘charter’d street’, and a version of the last stanza ending ‘smites with plagues the Marriage hearse’. Third, the 1901 letterpress reprint gives ‘A mark’. Two witnesses, one of them the poet’s own draft, print a verb; the nineteenth-century reprint prints a noun. That is not proof of what the plate’s copper shows, but it is a reason to trust ‘And mark’ and to treat ‘A mark’ as an editorial change introduced after Blake’s death. The rest of the collation supports the same picture: the plate and draft print ‘The mind-forg’d manacles’, ‘Every black’ning Church appalls’, ‘Runs in blood down Palace walls’, while the reprint prints ‘mind-forged’, ‘blackening’, ‘appals’ and ‘palace-walls’. Note which differences are inert — ‘appalls’ and ‘appals’ mean the same thing — and which are not: ‘A mark’ is the only one that rewrites a clause. A useful model response states the variant, names the witnesses, says which reading it adopts, and says what would change its mind; a response that simply calls the modern spelling ‘wrong’ has not yet made an argument [2][3].
lessons.question: Two witnesses to a line differ as ‘And mark’ and ‘A mark’. What is the strongest evidential use of that difference?
lessons.answer: Name both witnesses, show that the difference changes the clause’s subject and verb, and treat the noun reading as a posthumous editorial change that further witnesses can overturn
lessons.distractor: Prefer the older witness without discussion, because the earliest printing is always closest to the author’s intention
lessons.correction: Antiquity is a relevant consideration, not a rule, and it is worth saying why here: the draft and the plate transcription both give a verb, and the witness that gives the noun is a reprint made long after the poet’s death. But the argument has to be stated as an inference from named witnesses, with the ‘no scan’ limitation acknowledged, and with a sentence about what evidence would reverse it. ‘Earliest wins’ would reach the right answer for the wrong reason.

depth.definitions: A textual variant is a place where witnesses to the same work differ in wording, punctuation or spelling. A witness is any document that carries the text — an author’s draft, a printed edition, a transcription, a manuscript copy. Collation is the systematic comparison of witnesses. A plate text is the wording engraved on a Blake plate, which might differ from any printed edition made from it. Elision is the dropping of a syllable in pronunciation, often cued in print by an apostrophe, as in ‘charter’d’. Prerequisites: lesson 40 on symbol, over-reading and the defensible claim, and lesson 37 on line-by-line reading; the distinction between a report about an author’s intention and an interpretive claim comes from lesson 40.
depth.mechanism: Variants matter in proportion to what they change. Four grades are worth separating. Orthographic variants (‘appalls’ against ‘appals’, ‘palace-walls’ against ‘Palace walls’) alter the look of the page and can alter emphasis but not the sentence. Elision cues (‘charter’d’ against ‘chartered’) alter the reader’s performance of the line while leaving its sense intact; the apostrophe is a metrical instruction, and the modern spelling removes the instruction without altering the underlying count of eight syllables in the line ‘I wander thro’ each charter’d street’. Personification cues are capitalisation, which in the plate marks ‘Man’, ‘Church’, ‘Soldier’ and ‘Harlot’ as agents; lowercasing them demotes them towards background. Grammatical variants — ‘And mark’ against ‘A mark’ — are the most consequential, because they change which entity is the subject of a verb, and therefore change what the poem reports as happening. The mechanism to carry away is that editorial change is cumulative and directional: a reprint that normalises spelling usually also normalises grammar and personification, so that the cumulative effect can be a different poem, not merely a tidier one.
depth.secondExample: Apply the same four grades to a second poem from this level, Keats’s ‘Ode on a Grecian Urn’. Between the 1820 volume as reprinted by Project Gutenberg and the 1884 Poetical Works transcribed on Wikisource, you can observe ‘Thou still unravish’d bride of quietness,’ against ‘Thou still unravish’d bride of quietness!’, ‘leaf-fring’d’ against ‘leaf-fringed’, ‘For ever wilt thou love’ against ‘Forever wilt thou love’, and ‘What maiden’s loth’ style punctuation differences in the fourth line of the first stanza. The exclamation mark after ‘quietness’ is not orthography: it converts an address into an exclamation, which changes the tone of the opening. Both witnesses, however, agree on the punctuation of the final two lines, which is why the question raised in lesson 65 is a genuine crux rather than an artefact of one careless editor.
depth.mistake: The common misconception is that spelling and punctuation are pre-argument decoration, so that the only real interpretive questions are about imagery and theme. Diagnose it by asking what the poem’s first sentence is about: if the answer changes when the third word of a clause changes from a verb to a noun, then the variant is doing argumentative work. A second misconception is the reverse — treating every difference as meaningful. ‘Appals’ and ‘appalls’ are the same word; claiming otherwise inflates the evidence and weakens the parts of the argument that do hold. The diagnostic question for both errors is the same: what, precisely, would be read differently?
depth.application: Nonblocking task: collate the fourth stanza of ‘London’ across the plate transcription and the 1901 reprint, then write 150 words that (a) lists every difference, (b) grades each one as orthographic, elisional, personifying or grammatical, and (c) states one interpretive consequence of the grammatical grade, if there is one. Model response, self-reviewed: ‘The plate prints “the hapless Soldier’s sigh” and “Runs in blood down Palace walls”; the reprint prints the same with “palace-walls” hyphenated and lowercased. The hyphenation and the lower case are personification and typographic cues; the clause is unchanged. The one grammatical variant in the poem is in stanza one. Because the fourth stanza has no grammatical variant, the only defensible interpretive claim about it concerns emphasis rather than agency.’ A satisfactory answer names witnesses and grades differences; an excellent answer withdraws a claim it cannot support.
depth.summary: Read at the scale of the word and you find that editorial decisions are interpretive decisions. The practical discipline is to name the witness, grade the difference, and state what would change your mind — the same discipline that lessons 65 to 70 apply to whole poems and to critical arguments.

visual.description: A four-row comparison grid in which the plate transcription, the 1793 draft and the 1901 reprint are lined up clause by clause so that the single grammatical variant can be separated from spelling and typographic noise.

Row 2 — the crux: ‘And mark in every face I meet’ / ‘And [see del.] mark in every face I meet’ (draft) / ‘A mark in every face I meet’: grammatical, because the clause gains or loses a verb

Ask of each row: who is the subject, and what work does the reader do? Only row 2 changes the answer
State the conclusion with its limit: two of three witnesses print a verb, but the plate witness is a transcription with no scan attached

lessons.title: The line against the sentence: enjambment and suspended syntax in Paradise Lost, Book I
lessons.explanation: A line is a unit of measure; a sentence is a unit of grammar. When the two do not coincide, the reader’s ear is told to pause where the syntax has not finished, and that disagreement is enjambment. Milton makes the disagreement into a procedure and defends it in print. In the note on ‘The Verse’ prefixed to the poem, transcribed from the 1674 printing on Wikisource, he writes that his measure ‘is English Heroic Verse without Rime as that of Homer in Greek, and of Virgil in Latin’, that rime is ‘no necessary Adjunct or true Ornament of Poem or good Verse’, and that the music of his verse ‘consists only in apt Numbers, fit quantity of Syllables, and the sense variously drawn out from one Verse into another, not in the jingling sound of like endings’. The phrase to keep is the last one: the sense is drawn out from one verse into another. Count the suspension in the poem’s opening. The first sentence is not a sentence about disobedience; it is a purpose-clause whose main verb arrives six lines in: ‘Of Man’s first disobedience, and the fruit / Of that forbidden tree whose mortal taste / Brought death into the World, and all our woe, / With loss of Eden, till one greater Man / Restore us, and regain the blissful seat, / Sing, Heavenly Muse, that, on the secret top / Of Oreb, or of Sinai, didst inspire / That shepherd who first taught the chosen seed’. Read the line-endings alone and you hear six stops; read the syntax alone and there is no stop before ‘Sing’. The whole aim of the sentence — ‘That, to the height of this great argument, / I may assert Eternal Providence, / And justify the ways of God to men’ — is the last thing you reach [1][2].
lessons.example: Take the two hardest cases in the book’s first fifty lines and work them as arguments about effect rather than as impressions. Case one is the interrupted question in lines 27 to 36: ‘Say first--for Heaven hides nothing from thy view, / Nor the deep tract of Hell--say first what cause / Moved our grand parents, in that happy state, / Favoured of Heaven so highly, to fall off / From their Creator, and transgress his will / For one restraint, lords of the World besides. / Who first seduced them to that foul revolt? / Th’ infernal Serpent; he it was whose guile, / Stirred up with envy and revenge, deceived / The mother of mankind’. The speaker begins a question, breaks it for a parenthetical oath, begins it again with the same words ‘say first’, completes it, adds a second question, and answers both with a two-word identification before the sentence is finished. The line-endings fall in the middle of the delay, so the pause marks not a thought completed but a thought withheld. Case two is the inversion at lines 44 to 47: ‘Him the Almighty Power / Hurled headlong flaming from th’ ethereal sky, / With hideous ruin and combustion, down / To bottomless perdition’. The object sits at the end of one line, its agent and verb at the start of the next, and the prepositional phrase ‘To bottomless perdition’ arrives after two lines of turbulence. The rival explanation must be stated in its strongest form: Milton is imitating Latin word order, and a reader who knows Latin hears nothing more than respectable syntax; on that account the fall of the sentence across the line is a side-effect of a borrowed grammar rather than a designed effect. The interpretive question is then which account explains more — including the note on ‘The Verse’, where the poet himself advertises the technique as a virtue [1].
lessons.question: A student writes: ‘Milton’s enjambment imitates natural speech, which is why the sentences run past the lines.’ What is the main difficulty with that claim?
lessons.answer: Milton’s own defence rests on the opposite of natural speech, since he claims a recovered ancient liberty and a music of apt numbers rather than the jingling of rhyme, and the suspensions are longer and more contrived than speech
lessons.distractor: There is no difficulty, because enjambment always reflects the rhythms of spoken language
lessons.correction: Enjambment can imitate speech, but in this poem the technique is theorised in print as an art derived from Homer and Virgil and set against rhyme; the point of the note on ‘The Verse’ is that the reader should attend to numbers and quantities, not to conversational ease. The suspensions of five and six lines in the opening are also far longer than any speech unit, so the claim fails on both the documentary and the descriptive evidence.

depth.definitions: Enjambment is the continuation of a syntactic unit past the end of a line of verse; the opposite is a line whose end coincides with a syntactic boundary. Suspension is the delay of a required element — often the main verb — across several lines, so that the reader holds an incomplete structure. Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter. Heroic verse, in Milton’s phrasing, is the verse of epic. A purpose clause (‘That … I may assert’) states the aim of the main clause. Prerequisites: lesson 38 on metre and form, and lesson 37 on line-by-line reading; the difference between a fact about syntax and a claim about effect is from lesson 40.
depth.mechanism: Holding a sentence open across a line break has three measurable consequences. It lengthens the reader’s working memory: six lines of subordinate material must be carried until ‘Sing’ supplies a verb, so the line-end pauses function as breaths rather than as logical stops. It redistributes emphasis: whatever falls immediately after the break is heard as arriving under pressure, which is why ‘Hurled headlong’ and ‘Sing’ land harder than they would mid-line. And it makes retrospection unavoidable: the reader who has finished line five cannot parse it until line six arrives, so the poem enforces a second pass — a rereading built into the metre. The limitation is that none of this is automatic. Enjambment is a real syntactic fact and can be counted in code; the claim that a particular suspension feels like hesitation or like falling is an interpretation, supported by the poet’s own note and by the pattern of use across the book, and stated as contestable.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a passage where Milton does the opposite: the opening of Book I line 27 to 29, as quoted above, suspends, but the famous description of the host in Book I lines 50 to 60 is built on clause-by-clause completion, with ‘Nine times the space that measures day and night / To mortal men, he, with his horrid crew, / Lay vanquished, rolling in the fiery gulf’ closing at the line-end. There, sentence and line agree, and the effect is a slow, level accounting suited to a catalogue of loss. The method generalises beyond Milton. In the 1901 Blake and 1826 Blake witnesses collated in lesson 61, the quatrain is end-stopped almost throughout, and the single grammatical variant in stanza one therefore carries the whole weight of the opening. Same technique, different distribution: where lines are closed, a single enjambment or a single syntactic variant becomes an event.
depth.mistake: The typical error is to treat enjambment as a mood-word rather than a structure, writing that the verse feels ‘flowing’ without identifying which phrase crosses which boundary. Diagnose by asking for the boundary and the phrase: if the writer cannot name both, there is no observation to evaluate. The second error is to claim that Latin syntax explains the inversions and therefore that no interpretation is warranted; the presence of a cause is not a demonstration that the effect is inert, and in this case the poem’s own prefatory note tells you the poet considered the technique a designed feature.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: take lines 1 to 26 and mark every place where a clause boundary crosses a line-end, then write 200 words arguing whether the first sentence’s long suspension prepares the reader for the assertion ‘And justify the ways of God to men’, with one sentence stating the counter-argument that the delay is merely Virgilian imitation. Model response, self-reviewed: ‘Four of the six line-ends in the opening six lines occur inside noun phrases … the suspension makes the reader supply the verb, so the assertion about Providence arrives as a completion the reader has been holding open … The counter-argument is that the same suspensions occur throughout Latin epic and carry no local emphasis; it is weakened, not refuted, by the prefatory note, and a full answer would collate two or three comparable suspensions elsewhere in Book I.’ A satisfactory answer names boundaries; an excellent one keeps the counter-argument alive.
depth.summary: Milton prints a theory of the line and then writes sentences that test it. Reading the disagreement between line and sentence is a transferable technique: it tells you where a poem expects you to pause, and where it expects you to continue, and those two instructions are the raw material of prosodic interpretation.

visual.title: Where the sentence breaks and where the line breaks: Paradise Lost, Book I, lines 1–6
visual.description: A two-track diagram of the poem’s opening, with the syntactic track running continuously and the metrical track stopping at every line-end, so that the six-line suspension of the verb can be seen rather than described.
steps: Metrical track: line 1 ends after ‘fruit’; line 2 after ‘taste’; line 3 after ‘woe’; line 4 after ‘Man’; line 5 after ‘seat’; line 6 contains the first main verb, ‘Sing’
Syntactic track: ‘Of Man’s first disobedience … till one greater Man / Restore us, and regain the blissful seat’ is all subordinate material; nothing is asserted yet
The collision: five line-end pauses are heard inside a structure that is not finished, so each pause is a breath, not a full stop
The turn: ‘Sing’ arrives at the head of line 6, immediately after the previous line-end, so the poem’s first action is an imperative addressed to the Muse
Second collision: lines 44–47 place the object ‘Him’ at a line-end and its agent and verb at the next line’s start
Counter-diagram: lines 50–52, where clause and line end together, to show what the poem sounds like when the two tracks agree

lessons.title: The extended conceit as argument: Donne’s compasses and Johnson’s objection
lessons.explanation: A conceit is a figure that is developed at length and that organises a whole passage rather than decorating one line. Donne’s ‘A Valediction: forbidding mourning’ ends on the best-known example in English, and the printed text in the Grierson edition on Project Gutenberg reads: ‘If they be two, they are two so / As stiffe twin compasses are two, / Thy soule the fixt foot, makes no show / To move, but doth, if the’other doe. / And though it in the center sit, / Yet when the other far doth rome, / It leanes, and hearkens after it, / And growes erect, as that comes home. / Such wilt thou be to mee, who must / Like th’other foot, obliquely runne; / Thy firmnes makes my circle just, / And makes me end, where I begunne.’ The figure is not a comparison of lovers to an instrument in the way a simile is; it is a machine with parts, and the parts have to correspond to the claim’s parts. The claim is that two souls are one (‘Our two soules therefore, which are one’) and that absence cannot breach that unity. The compasses can carry the claim because they have exactly two members, one that stays and one that travels, and because the traveller’s completion depends on the stayer: the moving foot draws a circle only if the fixed foot holds. The poem also shows what the figure costs. Earlier figures — melting, gold beaten to ‘ayery thinnesse’ — say that the lovers separate without breaking; the compasses go further and say that separation is what makes the union legible. That is a stronger claim and it is why the last couplet can be a proof rather than a farewell [1].
lessons.example: Set the figure against its best-attested hostile reading. In the Life of Cowley, in the 1891 Cassell edition on Project Gutenberg, Johnson defines a kind of wit as ‘a kind of discordia concors; a combination of dissimilar images, or discovery of occult resemblances in things apparently unlike’, and then delivers the sentence that has followed the metaphysicals ever since: ‘The most heterogeneous ideas are yoked by violence together’. His complaint is not that the figure is unclear but that clarity is not the point: ‘the reader commonly thinks his improvement dearly bought, and though he sometimes admires, is seldom pleased’. Now test the objection against this specific passage. The compasses are two things: a mating pair and a draughting instrument, and Johnson’s charge is that only violence holds them together. A defence can be precise about where the violence is. The correspondence of parts is exact, so the figure is not incongruous at the level of structure; what it does impose is a subordinate role on the woman, who is the fixed foot, and a rôle of wandering on the speaker, which is a claim about the relationship disguised as geometry. The strongest form of Johnson’s objection, therefore, is not that the image is remote but that the image’s internal relations smuggle in a moral hierarchy the poem never argues for. A reader who answers that the fixed foot is ‘the center’ and therefore honoured has answered an argument the poem makes; a reader who says nothing has left the objection standing [2].
lessons.question: What does the compasses figure add that the earlier melting and gold-beating figures do not?
lessons.answer: It supplies two distinct parts with distinct motions, so the separation itself becomes the mechanism that completes the union rather than a loss the union survives
lessons.distractor: It supplies a more dignified image, since a scientific instrument suits a serious poem about death better than melting metal does
lessons.correction: Dignity is a matter of register and cannot explain the placement of the figure as the poem’s conclusion. The melting and gold figures say the lovers are divided but not destroyed; the compasses add structure, since one member must stay for the other’s motion to draw anything at all. That is why the final couplet can present constancy as the cause of arrival, and it is the feature a hostile critic like Johnson attacks when he calls the association violent.

depth.definitions: A conceit is a developed, often surprising figure extended across a passage. A vehicle is the image used (compasses); a tenor is what it is applied to (the lovers’ relationship); a ground is the respect in which they correspond. Discordia concors, in Johnson’s use, is a discordant union of images. Hyperbole is exaggeration; here the poem’s hyperboles are astronomical and geometric. Prerequisites: lesson 40 on symbol and over-reading, and lesson 38 on metre; the distinction between a figure’s structure and its moral implications is new at this level.
depth.mechanism: An extended conceit argues in three moves. Selection: only figures with the right number of internal parts can carry a claim with two parts, which is why the compasses displace melting. Mapping: each part of the vehicle is assigned to a part of the tenor — fixed foot to the beloved, moving foot to the speaker, the drawn circle to the completed relationship — and the mapping must be consistent, or the figure collapses into wordplay. Inference: once the mapping holds, the figure licenses conclusions the earlier figures could not reach, such as ‘Thy firmnes makes my circle just’. The limitation to state in any essay is that the inference is only as good as the mapping, and the mapping is chosen by the poet. That is precisely Johnson’s point, and it is why the compasses passage is a better test case for his objection than any figure he actually quotes.
depth.secondExample: Apply the three moves to a figure from this level’s other poems. In Hopkins’s ‘God’s Grandeur’ the image is electrical and agricultural at once: divine presence ‘will flame out, like shining from shook foil’, and simultaneously ‘It gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil / Crushed’. Two vehicles, two industrial processes, and one tenor; the mapping is partial because the poem does not say which process corresponds to which divine action, and the reader must decide whether the two images are alternatives or stages. That is a different conceit problem: not violence of association but under-specification of the mapping. Comparing the two passages teaches the diagnostic question — is the figure’s structure carrying the argument, or is the argument being carried by the figure’s associations alone?
depth.mistake: Two misconceptions recur. The first is that an extended conceit is decoration that can be replaced by any equally striking image; the diagnostic is to try the substitution — replace the compasses with a lighthouse and ask whether the poem still proves that constancy completes a circle. The second is that Johnson’s objection can be answered by pointing out that the image is ingenious, which concedes his point. The objection is about the cost to the reader and the smuggled premise, not about ingenuity, and a good answer engages the cost.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: write 250 words that (a) states the mapping in the compasses stanza as a four-item list, (b) identifies one place where the mapping is not exact, and (c) answers Johnson’s objection with a reply that concedes at least one of his complaints. Model response, self-reviewed: ‘Fixed foot = beloved; moving foot = speaker; the drawn circle = the completed relationship; firmness of the fixed foot = constancy that ensures return. The mapping is inexact at “growes erect, as that comes home”, where the compasses’ behaviour at closure is a mechanical necessity rather than a choice, which removes the woman’s agency. Against Johnson, I concede that the association of instrument and marriage is remote and that the reader pays for the conceit in effort; I reply that the effort is repaid because the figure supplies the argument’s structure, and I note that Johnson’s own definition of discordia concors describes the figure accurately without yet showing it to be a fault.’ A satisfactory answer maps the parts; an excellent one finds the inexactness without abandoning the argument.
depth.summary: Ask of any figure what its internal parts are and whether those parts match the parts of the claim. Where they match, the figure is doing argumentative work; where they do not, the discrepancy is either an artefact of the poet’s choice or the point of the passage, and only evidence can settle which.

readings.note: Read the passage on ‘the metaphysical poets’, beginning with ‘Wit, like all other things subject by their nature to the choice of man, has its changes and fashions’. visual.title: Mapping a conceit’s parts: the compasses stanza against the poem’s claim

Claim 2 — absence does not breach the union: vehicle provides one member that does not move, so absence is assigned to the other member

Conclusion to state in writing: the figure does argumentative work and imposes a cost, and both facts belong in the analysis

lessons.title: Stress, ear and a poet’s own theory: Hopkins’s sprung rhythm in ‘God’s Grandeur’ and ‘The Windhover’
lessons.explanation: Hopkins is the rare case of a poet whose prosodic theory survives in print alongside the poems it governs — the Author’s Preface stands at the head of the 1918 volume — which means his metre can be checked against his own description rather than only against an editor’s labels. In the Author’s Preface printed in the 1918 edition of his Poems on Project Gutenberg, he writes: ‘Sprung Rhythm, as used in this book, is measured by feet of from one to four syllables, regularly, and for … particular effects any number of weak or slack syllables may be used.’ (The ellipsis marks a page number printed inside the sentence in this edition.) A little later he adds, in the note on the nature and history of sprung rhythm, that ‘Sprung Rhythm is the most natural of things’, and he claims that it is ‘the rhythm of common speech and of written prose, when rhythm is perceived in them’. Two consequences follow for the reader. First, the counting unit is the foot containing one stress, not the syllable, so a line may have four stresses and eleven syllables, and the syllable count will tell you very little. Second, because stresses can be packed together — ‘Generations have trod, have trod, have trod’ — the poem’s insistent effects are produced by adjacent stresses rather than by long vowels or rhyme. ‘God’s Grandeur’ begins with an assertion of presence (‘THE world is charged with the grandeur of God’) and then immediately converts presence into potential energy: ‘It will flame out, like shining from shook foil; / It gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil / Crushed.’ Three feet of one strong syllable each, in the phrase ‘shook foil’, sit inside a line the ear expects to flow, and the shock is structural rather than merely auditory [1].
lessons.example: Read ‘God’s Grandeur’ as a sonnet whose argument is carried by where the stresses fall. The octave runs through human damage — ‘Generations have trod, have trod, have trod; / And all is seared with trade; bleared, smeared with toil; / And wears man’s smudge and shares man’s smell: the soil / Is bare now, nor can foot feel, being shod’ — and two things are audible at once: the alliterative pile-up of monosyllables in ‘seared’, ‘trade’, ‘bleared’, ‘smeared’, ‘smudge’, ‘smell’, and the way the repeated ‘have trod’ converts a verb into a drumbeat. Then the volta: ‘And for all this, nature is never spent; / There lives the dearest freshness deep down things’. The claim turns on ‘And for all this’, five words that concede the whole indictment before answering it, and the answering line is the only one in the poem whose stresses are comparatively spaced out. The sestet closes with a suspension that is itself the argument: ‘Because the Holy Ghost over the bent / World broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings.’ The exclamation ‘ah!’ is a slack syllable doing expressive work — under Hopkins’s own rules any number of weak syllables may be used for particular effects, so the interjection is licensed by the theory rather than smuggled in. Now apply the same method to ‘The Windhover’, where the 1918 text prints compounds broken at the line-end: ‘morning’s minion, king- / dom of daylight’s dauphin, dapple-dawn-drawn Fal- / con, in his riding / Of the rolling level underneath him steady air’. The break inside ‘kingdom’ and inside ‘Falcon’ makes the reader pause where no word ends, so the metrical unit and the lexical unit disagree at exactly the point where the poem describes a bird’s suspended flight. A rival reading is available and should be stated: the hyphens may be a compositor’s convenience for a long line rather than a designed effect, and this edition’s text prints ‘ecstacy’ where modern editions print ‘ecstasy’, which is a reminder that you are reading an edition of 1918. The argument for the designed effect therefore rests on the density of the occurrences, not on one instance [1][2].
lessons.question: Under sprung rhythm, what determines the length of a line?
lessons.answer: The number of stressed feet, each carrying one stress and one to four syllables, so syllable totals vary while the stress pattern stays fixed
lessons.distractor: The number of syllables, since each foot contains exactly two, as in running rhythm
lessons.correction: Two-syllable feet describe running or common rhythm, which Hopkins contrasts with sprung rhythm in the same preface. In sprung rhythm the foot is defined by its one stress, and the syllable count may vary from one to four per foot, so scanning by syllables produces the wrong count and obscures the effects the poet is engineering.

depth.definitions: Metre is a patterned arrangement of stresses; scansion is the act of marking it. A foot is a metrical unit with one principal stress; a slack syllable is unstressed. Running or common rhythm is Hopkins’s term for the ordinary two- or three-syllable-foot English measure; sprung rhythm is his alternative, measured by feet of one to four syllables. Counterpoint rhythm is the mounting of a second rhythm on the first. Inscape, in Hopkins’s vocabulary, is a thing’s individuating form. Prerequisites: lesson 38 on metre and form, lesson 37 on line-by-line reading, and lesson 62 on the disagreement between line and syntax, which is the same technique applied to Milton.
depth.mechanism: Sprung rhythm changes three things at once. It makes stress rather than syllable count the organising unit, which is why a line can be scanned with four stresses and eleven syllables without becoming irregular. It permits clusters of stressed syllables, which is how ‘have trod, have trod, have trod’ can function as a repeated beat rather than as a phrase. And it licenses extreme slacks, so an interjection like ‘ah!’ can occupy the position of a slack syllable and still register as an event. The limitation to keep in view is that Hopkins’s theory is a producer’s account, not a neutral description; it tells you what he intended the reader to hear. A sceptical reading exists in the scholarly literature — the Victorian Web essay listed below puts it as a paraphrase rather than a quotation, namely that almost none of what Hopkins argued for was new in English poetry, and adds that ‘no other poet has since used sprung rhythm regularly’ — and that observation is a real qualification of the theoretical claim while leaving the local effects intact.
depth.secondExample: Use the same procedure on a poet who never wrote a preface. In Blake’s ‘London’, the quatrain’s fourth line has three stresses against the first three lines’ four, and the stresses are almost entirely monosyllabic: ‘Marks of weakness, marks of woe’. Nothing in the poem explains the pattern, so the reader must infer it from repetition across the sixteen lines, and any claim about its meaning is an interpretation. Hopkins supplies the theory and loses a degree of freedom: you cannot say the pattern is accidental, but you can ask whether the theory accounts for every effect it claims. Comparing the two is the fastest way to see how much interpretive work a poet’s own manifesto does for, and to, a reader.
depth.mistake: The usual error is to scan Hopkins’s lines by counting syllables and then declare the metre irregular or ‘free’. Diagnose it by applying the poet’s own definition: count stresses, not syllables, and see whether four or five stresses recur. A second error is to treat the published theory as proof of the poem’s quality; the theory explains a procedure, and it neither guarantees the procedure’s success nor establishes its novelty, which is a separate question the secondary reading addresses.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: scan the first eight lines of ‘God’s Grandeur’ by stress only, marking each foot as one, two, three or four syllables, then write 150 words on whether the octave’s stress pattern differs from the sestet’s, with one sentence on what the difference would mean if it does not exist. Model response, self-reviewed: ‘The octave is dominated by one- and two-syllable feet and by adjacent stresses in “seared”, “trade”, “bleared”, “smeared” … The sestet admits a three-syllable foot at “dearest freshness” and a four-syllable stretch around “with warm breast and with ah!” … If the counts were identical across octave and sestet, the volta would have to be argued on lexical and syntactical grounds alone, since metre could not be carrying it.’ A satisfactory answer counts stresses; an excellent one names what it would lose if the counts matched.
depth.summary: A poet’s own prosodic theory is both a gift and a trap: it supplies a vocabulary and a set of rules, and it tempts the reader to accept the poet’s account of novelty and effect. The discipline is to use the theory to scan, then to test the theory’s claims against the poems and against other readers.

visual.title: Stress before syllables: scanning a sprung-rhythm octave and sestet
visual.description: A scan diagram of ‘God’s Grandeur’ in which every foot is marked with one stress and a syllable count, so that clusters of stress and stretches of slack can be compared between octave and sestet.
steps: Line 1 — assertion: stresses on ‘world’, ‘charged’, ‘grand’, ‘God’; feet mostly three syllables, so the line feels level
Line 6 — cluster: ‘seared’, ‘trade’, ‘bleared’, ‘smeared’ pile four stresses into a short span, which no two-syllable-foot measure permits easily
Line 5 — repetition: ‘have trod, have trod, have trod’ converts a verb into a beat, so the stress pattern carries the moral complaint
Line 9 — volta: ‘And for all this’ concedes before it answers; its stresses are the sparsest in the poem
Line 14 — slack licensed by theory: ‘with ah! bright wings’ sets an interjection where a pause would otherwise fall
Test applied — count stresses per line, not syllables; then ask whether the sestet’s pattern differs from the octave’s, and what the analysis loses if it does not

lessons.title: The whole poem as one claim: Keats’s ‘Ode on a Grecian Urn’ and the line that speaks
lessons.explanation: Reading a whole poem as one argument means asking what the poem asserts, what it merely asks, and which voice does the asserting — and then checking whether the text you have actually answers that last question. Keats’s ‘Ode on a Grecian Urn’ begins as an address to a thing that cannot answer: ‘Thou still unravish’d bride of quietness, / Thou foster-child of silence and slow time, / Sylvan historian, who canst thus express / A flowery tale more sweetly than our rhyme’ (1820 volume text, as reprinted by Project Gutenberg). The first stanza is almost entirely questions (‘What leaf-fring’d legend haunts about thy shape … What men or gods are these? What maidens loth?’), and the poem’s middle stanzas continue with paradoxes rather than statements: ‘Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter’, and ‘For ever wilt thou love, and she be fair!’. The urn’s advantage is stated as a lack — the figures cannot age because they cannot finish anything. Only in the fifth stanza does a general claim appear: ‘Thou, silent form, dost tease us out of thought / As doth eternity: Cold Pastoral!’, and then the two lines that have been argued over since 1820: ‘“Beauty is truth, truth beauty,”--that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know.’ Look at the punctuation in the two witnesses below. Both print an opening quotation mark before ‘Beauty’ and close it after ‘truth beauty,’ — so in both, the words ‘that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know’ fall outside the urn’s reported speech. The poem therefore leaves undetermined whether the urn says the whole sentence or only its first half, and a reading that asserts either must say so as an inference with evidence [1][2].
lessons.example: Build the whole-poem argument, then test it on the crux. Step one, form: the ode runs five ten-line stanzas with a rhyme scheme that keeps turning back on itself, and the fifth stanza’s final couplet is the only place where the poem stops asking and asserts. Step two, content: the poem’s four stanzas of address establish a contrast between living passion which ‘leaves a heart high-sorrowful and cloy’d’ and art which is ‘For ever warm and still to be enjoy’d’. Step three, tension: the same permanence is described as ‘Cold Pastoral!’, so the poem’s own evaluation of the state it praises is divided — the exclamation can be admiration or recoil, and the syntax does not settle it. Step four, the crux: if the urn speaks the whole final sentence, the poem ends with an object instructing the reader about knowledge, which sits oddly with four stanzas in which the urn could not answer anything; if the urn speaks only ‘Beauty is truth, truth beauty’, the last two lines are the poet’s own voice ventriloquising the urn, and the poem ends on a claim that the poet has not earned elsewhere. Both readings can be defended. Collation sharpens the question because the witnesses differ in their punctuation elsewhere in the poem: the 1820 volume text has ‘Thou still unravish’d bride of quietness,’ while the 1884 Poetical Works transcribed on Wikisource prints ‘quietness!’, and the 1884 text prints ‘Thou, silent form! dost tease us out of thought’ where the 1820 volume prints ‘Thou, silent form, dost tease us out of thought’. Since the two witnesses disagree about the force of address in three places, the fact that they agree about the quotation marks in the last two lines is real evidence — evidence about what the 1884 editor saw in the 1820 volume, and not proof about Keats’s manuscript. One further claim circulates: a university teaching page states that the version printed in the Annals of the Fine Arts in the same year carries no quotation marks at all. I could not fetch that printing, so it is recorded here as a claim by that page and nothing more, which is exactly how an unresolved textual question should be handled in an essay [1][2][3].
lessons.question: Both fetched witnesses print ‘“Beauty is truth, truth beauty,”--that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know.’ What follows for interpretation?
lessons.answer: The closing quotation mark falls before the final two lines, so the text does not settle who speaks them, and any claim about the urn’s or the poet’s voice must be argued rather than cited
lessons.distractor: The urn speaks all three lines, since the whole passage follows the poet’s address to the urn and the quotation marks enclose the sentence
lessons.correction: The quotation marks do not enclose the sentence; they close after ‘truth beauty,’ and ‘that is all / Ye know on earth…’ lies outside them in both witnesses checked. The reading that the urn speaks everything may be defensible, but it cannot be produced by pointing at punctuation that does not say so; the correct form is an argument from the poem’s structure, with the punctuation given its true state.

depth.definitions: An ode is a lyric poem of elevated address; a crux is a passage where the text is disputed or where the sense cannot be settled without interpretation. A witness is a document carrying the text (see lesson 61). Address is the poem’s turning towards a listener or object — here, the urn. Apostrophe is address to an absent or inanimate thing. A volta is a turn in argument, usually marked in sonnets and often unmarked in odes. Prerequisites: lessons 37, 38 and 40 on form, metre and the defensible claim, and lesson 61 on collation.
depth.mechanism: Whole-poem argument works by converting a list of observations into a structure with dependencies. The claim must explain why the poem’s questions precede its answers, why its praises of permanence are also complaints, and why the final couplet’s register is more proverbial than the stanzas that precede it. The crux functions as a test: if a reading of the whole poem requires the urn to speak all three lines, the reading is exposed to the punctuation evidence, which neither supports nor refutes it. The limitation to state is that punctuation in an 1820 volume is a compositor’s work as well as a poet’s, so an argument from a comma is weaker than an argument from a clause distribution that survives across witnesses — and where the witnesses disagree, as they do at ‘quietness’ and at ‘silent form’, the reader must say which witness carries the claim.
depth.secondExample: Run the same test on Shelley’s ‘Ozymandias’ in the next lesson’s comparison. There the words spoken by the statue are unambiguously quoted inside the traveller’s report: the 1818 Examiner text gives ‘“My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings.”’ followed by ‘Look on my works ye Mighty, and despair!’, and the 1819 text keeps the report but moves the closing quotation mark, so that the despairing command falls inside the speech. The difference between the two poems is instructive: Shelley’s crux is inside the architecture of a framed report, whereas Keats’s crux concerns whether a reported speaker or the poet is speaking at all. In both cases the discipline is identical — describe the punctuation you actually have, name the witness, and then argue.
depth.mistake: The inherited misconception is that the ode’s last two lines are simply ‘the urn’s message’, repeated in thousands of summaries. Diagnose it by asking which edition the summary used and what its quotation marks enclose; in the two witnesses fetched here, they do not enclose the last two lines. The opposite error is to conclude that the passage is therefore meaningless or that Keats was careless. A textual crux is a place where interpretation must do work, not a defect, and it is perfectly possible for the strongest reading to be one in which the poem deliberately leaves the voice unsettled.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: write 250 words arguing for one answer to the crux — urn, poet, or deliberate indeterminacy — using at least two pieces of internal evidence and one statement of what textual evidence would change your mind. Model response, self-reviewed: ‘The fifth stanza’s first eight lines are addressed to the urn, and the urn is credited with saying only “Beauty is truth, truth beauty”. The final two lines use “Ye”, a plural address that appears nowhere else in the poem, which suggests a change of addressee and therefore a change of speaker. Internal evidence: the poem’s four earlier stanzas never let the urn speak, so a sudden two-line lecture from the urn would be unmotivated. I would abandon the reading if a manuscript witness showed the quotation marks enclosing all three lines; the 1820 volume and the 1884 edition both close them earlier.’ A satisfactory answer commits; an excellent one names the evidence that would move it.
depth.summary: A poem’s meaning is not the sum of its images but the dependency structure of its claims and questions — and where the text is a crux, the honest essay reports the state of the evidence instead of borrowing a conclusion from habit.

visual.title: Questions, paradoxes and the crux: the five-stanza structure of the ‘Ode on a Grecian Urn’
visual.description: A stanza-by-stanza diagram of the ode tracking whether each stanza asks, praises or asserts, ending in a quotation-mark diagram of the disputed final couplet.
steps: Stanza 1 — questions only: ‘What leaf-fring’d legend’, ‘What men or gods are these?’; the poem addresses a silent object
Stanza 2 — paradox stated: ‘Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter’; the urn’s gain is a form of loss
Stanza 3 — accumulation: ‘For ever warm and still to be enjoy’d’ builds a permanence that the stanza’s own words make feverish
Stanza 4 — the town emptied: the urn’s permanence is now described as desolation, which complicates any simple praise
Stanza 5 — the only assertion: ‘Thou, silent form, dost tease us out of thought / As doth eternity: Cold Pastoral!’
Crux diagram: opening quotation mark before ‘Beauty is truth’, closing mark after ‘truth beauty,’; the final two lines lie outside the marks in both witnesses fetched, so the speaker is undetermined

questions.prompt: An editor preparing a school anthology of Blake’s ‘London’ decides to print ‘A mark in every face I meet’ because that reading appears in a widely used 1901 edition, and adds a note saying the wording is identical in all sources. A reviewer objects. Which objection is best supported by the evidence available?
questions.answer: The note is false and the choice is consequential: the plate transcription and the poet’s own draft both print a verb, and the noun reading changes which entity governs the clause
questions.distractor: The note is false because no two witnesses ever agree in early modern printing, so the editor should have collated at least twenty copies before printing
questions.correction: The reviewer’s point is not that collation was insufficiently wide but that the two named witnesses support the other reading and that the difference is grammatical rather than cosmetic. Claiming universal agreement is a factual error, and choosing the noun reading on the authority of a single posthumous reprint quietly converts an editorial decision into an interpretive one.

questions.prompt: A student analyses a blank-verse passage and reports that the poet ‘breaks the lines to create a feeling of disorder’. Asked to support the claim, the student points to a line that ends with a comma. What is the most useful diagnosis?
questions.answer: No boundary has been identified: the claim needs a named phrase crossing a named line-end, and a comma at the line-end marks a pause where syntax and line agree
questions.distractor: The claim is fine, because any line ending in punctuation signals tension between metre and meaning
questions.correction: The evidential unit in prosody is the boundary, not the mood: a reader must be able to say which syntactic unit crosses which line-end, as with the five-line suspension before ‘Sing’ in Paradise Lost, Book I. A comma at a line-end is the opposite case, since the pause and the syntax coincide; treating it as disorder inverts the observation the claim requires.

questions.prompt: An essay argues that Donne’s compasses ‘show how much the lovers love each other’, citing the figure’s beauty. A tutor asks for the mapping. Which answer would most nearly satisfy the demand?
questions.answer: Fixed foot is the beloved, moving foot is the speaker, the drawn circle is the completed relationship, and constancy in the fixed foot is what makes the completion possible
questions.distractor: The compasses are a technical instrument, so the figure shows that the love is precise, measured and rational rather than emotional
questions.correction: The second answer reads a property of the vehicle as though it were a property of the tenor and never builds the correspondence. The first answer supplies the parts and their relations, which is what an argument from a conceit requires, and it also exposes the place where the mapping is inexact, since the moving foot’s return is mechanical while the poem’s fidelity is chosen.

questions.prompt: A reader scans ‘God’s Grandeur’ by counting syllables, finds that the lines vary between nine and eleven, and concludes that the poem is unmetred. Which correction is best?
questions.answer: Sprung rhythm is measured by stressed feet of one to four syllables, so a variable syllable count is compatible with a fixed pattern of stresses, which must be counted instead
questions.distractor: The lines are unmetred, since a regular English line must keep a constant syllable count as in running rhythm
questions.correction: The reader has applied the rules of common rhythm to a poem whose theory of rhythm is printed with it. Counting stresses rather than syllables shows recurring four- and five-stress lines, and the variation in slack syllables is precisely the licence Hopkins describes ‘for particular effects’. The error is not in the counting but in the unit being counted.

questions.prompt: A study guide states that the urn in Keats’s ode ‘delivers its famous message: Beauty is truth, truth beauty, that is all ye know on earth’. A careful student checks two witnesses and finds the closing quotation mark after ‘truth beauty,’ in both. What follows?
questions.answer: The guide has asserted a speaker the text does not assign; the last two lines lie outside the quotation marks in the witnesses checked, so the question of voice must be argued rather than assumed
questions.distractor: The guide is right in substance, because quotation marks in a nineteenth-century volume are compositor’s marks and carry no evidential weight
questions.correction: Dismissing punctuation entirely is as unhelpful as resting a whole reading on it. What the check establishes is a limit: these witnesses place the final two lines outside the urn’s speech, so the guide’s flat attribution is not supported by them, and any argument about voice must proceed from the poem’s structure and must name the printed evidence, including its weakness.

units.title: Arguing about poems: comparison, adverse cases, replies and your own sustained case

lessons.title: Grounds for comparison: two ‘Ozymandias’ sonnets and Shelley’s two texts
lessons.explanation: Comparison is only as good as its ground — the respect in which two works are being compared. Shelley and his friend Horace Smith each wrote a sonnet on the same subject: Shelley’s was printed in The Examiner, whose page gives the date 11 January 1818, and the Wikisource transcription of Smith’s poem records that it was published in the same magazine a month later. The Wikisource transcription of the first printing in The Examiner gives Shelley’s poem beginning ‘I met a Traveller from an antique land, / Who said, “Two vast and trunkless legs of stone / Stand in the desart’ and ending ‘Look on my works ye Mighty, and despair! / No thing beside remains. Round the decay / Of that Colossal Wreck, boundless and bare, / The lone and level sands stretch far away.’ It is signed ‘Glirastes’. Smith’s sonnet, transcribed on Wikisource from a later collection, begins in the desert rather than in a report of it — ‘In Egypt’s sandy silence, all alone, / Stands a gigantic Leg, which far off throws / The only shadow that the Desert knows’ — gives the inscription as direct speech from the stone itself, ‘“I am great Ozymandias,” saith the stone’, and then, in its closing six lines, turns the moral on England: ‘We wonder,—and some Hunter may express / Wonder like ours, when thro’ the wilderness / Where London stood, holding the Wolf in chace, / He meets some fragment huge, and stops to guess / What powerful but unrecorded race / Once dwelt in that annihilated place.’ The ground of comparison is therefore unusually clean: same occasion, same form, same subject, same length, and one crucial structural difference — Shelley encloses the whole scene inside a reported speech by an unnamed traveller, while Smith narrates it directly and then applies it [1][2].
lessons.example: Use the two texts of Shelley’s own poem to show how much turns on one word and one mark of punctuation. The 1818 Examiner text has ‘My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings.’ inside quotation marks, then, outside them, ‘Look on my works ye Mighty, and despair!’ The 1819 text printed with Rosalind and Helen has ‘“My name is Ozymandias, king of kings: / Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!”’ — the colon and the moved closing mark place the despairing command inside the king’s reported speech. The 1819 text also closes the sentence as ‘Nothing beside remains’, where the 1818 text reads ‘No thing beside remains’. That is not a spelling difference: ‘no thing’ keeps ‘thing’ as a noun with a negation, while ‘nothing’ is a single pronoun, and the effect of the line shifts from a residual absence of one particular thing to total vacancy. A modern critical edition adds a third piece of evidence: the Project Gutenberg Complete Poetical Works prints ‘Nothing beside remains’, dates the poem to the Examiner, and notes a manuscript variant for line 9, where the Bodleian manuscript reads ‘this legend clear’ in place of ‘these words appear’. Now compare Smith’s sonnet on the same two points. Smith’s inscription is a boast spoken by the statue and his poem ends by naming London, so the moral has a target; Shelley’s traveller never mentions England, and the poem’s last line is sand. The comparison yields a claim you can defend: Shelley’s frame and his refusal to apply the lesson are doing the same work, since distance is what the poem is about. Smith’s sonnet, by contrast, spends its frame on a different device — a future hunter — and so must name its own city. Neither poem is thereby better; they solve the same problem two ways [3][4].
lessons.question: Which formulation states the comparison’s ground most usefully?
lessons.answer: Two sonnets written on one occasion treat one subject and one inscription, and differ principally in whether the scene is reported by an anonymous traveller or narrated directly with an application to a modern city
lessons.distractor: Two Romantic sonnets about Egypt show that Romantic poets of the same generation were interested in ruins and empire
lessons.correction: The second statement is true and almost useless: it identifies a shared topic but no point of difference that can be argued about. A ground of comparison must name the respect in which the works are alike and the respect in which they diverge, so that evidence on both sides bears on the same question. Here the organising difference is the frame and its consequences, and the shared subject matter is what makes that difference observable.

depth.definitions: A ground of comparison is the respect in which two works are compared; a frame is a narrative device placing one account inside another. Reported speech is speech presented by another speaker. A crux is a disputed passage (lesson 65). Collation is systematic comparison of witnesses (lesson 61). Prerequisites: lessons 34 and 45 on frames and unreliable narration, lesson 49 on comparing two texts with evidence, and lesson 61 on witnesses.
depth.mechanism: Comparison works by holding variables constant and then explaining variation. Because the two sonnets share occasion, form, subject and approximate date, any difference in effect is more plausibly attributable to structure than to period or taste. The frame is the structural variable: testimony at second hand cannot specify what the traveller did not see, so Shelley’s poem cannot mention London, and its silence about England is a consequence of its narrative choice rather than a political abstention. Smith’s direct narration can name the Wolf and the wilderness by the Thames, and so can moralise. The limitation is that a single pair of poems cannot establish a general rule about frames; what it can establish is that the frame is doing work in this poem, which is a claim about this poem and no more.
depth.secondExample: Test the frame’s consequences against a different pairing from an earlier lesson: two translations of the same Odyssey passage, or Lamb’s prose paraphrase of Macbeth against Shakespeare’s verse. In the Lamb case a change of medium removes the metre and part of the character’s interiority, so the comparison isolates medium rather than narrative structure. Applying that lesson here: if you want to compare Shelley and Smith, you should also be able to say what a change of medium would do to the same content — for instance, a prose paraphrase of Shelley’s sonnet retains the frame and still cannot name London, which shows that the frame is doing the work rather than the verse form.
depth.mistake: The usual error is to compare works on a topic — ‘both poems are about the transience of power’ — and then to treat shared themes as the analysis. Diagnose it by asking what a shared theme predicts: nothing, since both poems also share the alphabet. The second error is to treat one poem as the successful version and the other as the failed attempt, which replaces comparison with ranking and usually eliminates the very difference that makes the pair worth reading.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: write 300 words comparing the two sonnets on the single variable of who speaks the inscription, quoting one line from each and naming the witness for each quotation. Model response, self-reviewed: ‘Shelley’s 1818 text gives the inscription as “My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings.” and leaves the despairing line outside the quotation marks, so a reader may attribute it to the traveller or to the king; Smith’s text gives “I am great Ozymandias,” saith the stone, leaving no ambiguity of speaker. Since Shelley’s whole scene is already reported speech, an ambiguity at second hand deepens the distance the frame creates. I note that the 1819 text of Shelley’s poem moves the closing quotation mark, which shows that even this local question has a textual history, and I name the printing I quoted.’ A satisfactory answer isolates a variable; an excellent one names its witnesses and its uncertainty.
depth.summary: Choose the ground before you choose the evidence. A comparison that isolates one structural variable produces a claim you can test; a comparison that lists shared themes produces a paragraph you cannot defend.

lessons.title: Making the adverse case: Peacock on poetry and Johnson on ‘Lycidas’
lessons.explanation: An adverse reading is a reading against a text, and it is worth studying because the strongest objections often come from inside the tradition rather than from ignorance. Two public-domain examples make the pair. In 1820 Thomas Love Peacock, himself a poet, published a satire whose thesis is that poetry has become a redundant activity. It opens with a scheme: ‘Poetry, like the world, may be said to have four ages, but in a different order: the first age of poetry being the age of iron; the second, of gold; the third, of silver; and the fourth, of brass.’ The modern poet appears as a social anachronism: ‘A poet in our times is a semi-barbarian in a civilized community’, and ‘The march of his intellect is like that of a crab, backward.’ Peacock’s supporting argument is comparative rather than merely rude: poetry once occupied the whole field of intellect — ‘Poetry was the mental rattle that awakened the attention of intellect in the infancy of civil society’ — and now competes with mathematics, astronomy, chemistry and political economy. His peroration predicts that ‘the subordinacy of the ornamental to the useful will be more and more seen and acknowledged’, and that the decay of poetry will be recognised as dramatic poetry’s decay already is. In the Life of Milton, Samuel Johnson had earlier performed a narrower operation on a single canonical poem. Of ‘Lycidas’ he writes: ‘of which the diction is harsh, the rhymes uncertain, and the numbers unpleasing’, adding that ‘It is not to be considered as the effusion of real passion; for passion runs not after remote allusions and obscure opinions’, and, most memorably, ‘Where there is leisure for fiction, there is little grief’ [1][2].
lessons.example: Analyse each adverse case by naming its premise and asking what evidence would refute it. Johnson’s premise is a criterion: elegy must be the expression of real passion, and real passion does not reach for ornament. That premise is testable in principle, since it predicts that a mourner’s poetry will be bare, and Johnson himself supplies the test when he contrasts the pastoral apparatus with Cowley’s lines about studying together. He also concedes a great deal — ‘What beauty there is we must therefore seek in the sentiments and images’ — and, of the pastoral form, writes that ‘Its form is that of a pastoral; easy, vulgar, and therefore disgusting’, which shows that his objection is to a genre’s conventions as much as to one poem. Peacock’s premise is different in kind: he assumes that value is measurable by the progress of knowledge and that poetry’s share of the reading public must decline as useful study advances. That premise is an empirical prediction, and it has been refuted, in the plain sense that poetry has not ceased to be written or read. Notice also a difference between an adverse reading and a transcription error — a distinction worth practising on Peacock’s text here. The Wikisource transcription prints ‘taking a retrograde stride to the barbarisms and erude traditions of the age of iron’, where the sense requires ‘rude’. I could not consult the 1820 printing, so I record the oddity as what it is: a probable transcription artefact, not a witness variant of the kind lesson 61 taught you to weigh. Handling the two cases differently is the point of the exercise, since a variant is evidence about a text and an artefact is evidence about a transcriber [1][2].
lessons.question: Peacock predicts that the decay of poetry will soon be generally recognised. Which feature makes that prediction unlike Johnson’s objection to ‘Lycidas’?
lessons.answer: It is an empirical forecast about reception that can be checked against what happened next, whereas Johnson’s objection rests on a criterion for elegy that must be argued on evaluative grounds
lessons.distractor: It is less polite in tone, which is why Peacock’s essay is satire and Johnson’s is criticism
lessons.correction: Tone distinguishes the essays but does not distinguish the kinds of claim they make. Johnson offers a standard and applies it, so answering him means contesting the standard or the application. Peacock commits himself to a future fact, so answering him can be partly a matter of record: poetry continued to be written and read, and the predicted disappearance did not occur, though the prediction can be rescued in weaker forms.

depth.definitions: An adverse reading argues against a text or a class of texts. A premise is an unstated or stated proposition on which an argument depends; a criterion is a standard of judgement. Satire is writing that attacks by ridicule. Rebuttal answers an argument; refutation shows its premise false. A transcription artefact is an error introduced in copying, distinct from a variant, which is a genuine difference between witnesses. Prerequisites: lesson 58 on the critic’s job, lesson 63 on Johnson’s objection to metaphysical wit, and lesson 61 on witnesses.
depth.mechanism: Adverse cases persuade by three mechanisms, and it helps to know which is operating. First, criterion-shifting: a new standard is introduced under which the work fails, and the reader’s agreement depends on accepting the standard. Second, re-description: the work’s virtues are re-named as vices, as when the pastoral’s ease becomes vulgarity. Third, prediction: a claim about the future of the art, which converts a preference into a historical law. The limitation of all three is that they are answerable — criteria can be contested, re-descriptions can be reversed, predictions can be falsified — and an essay that adopts an adverse reading must say which of the three it is using and where it would break.
depth.secondExample: Try the same analysis on an adverse judgement from this level’s own material: the charge that Keats’s final couplet is a platitude rather than a conclusion. The critic’s premise is that a poem’s last line must be earned by the argument that precedes it; the re-description converts a summary into a slogan; the prediction, if any, would be about the poem’s standing with later readers, and history has not cooperated. Comparing that case with Peacock’s shows the same three mechanisms at work on a much smaller object, and it also shows why adverse readings are useful: each one tells you exactly what a poem must do to be good, and a reader who can answer the objection understands the poem better than a reader who has never met it.
depth.mistake: Two errors. The first is to answer an adverse case by praising the work harder — pointing out that ‘Lycidas’ is admired — which meets no premise. The second is to accept the adverse case wholesale because it is clever, which usually means importing the critic’s criterion without noticing. The diagnostic for both: state the critic’s premise in one sentence and then say whether you accept it, reject it, or accept it and argue about the application.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: in 250 words, reconstruct Peacock’s argument as a numbered chain of premises and conclusion, identify the weakest link, and state one piece of evidence that would test it. Model response, self-reviewed: ‘Premise 1: the value of an activity is a function of its contribution to useful knowledge. Premise 2: poetry contributed to knowledge when it was the sole repository of learning. Premise 3: poetry no longer contributes, since mathematics and political economy have taken the field. Conclusion: poetry’s readership and standing must decline. The weakest link is premise 1, which is assumed rather than argued and would be denied by anyone who thinks pleasure is a good; the testable part is premise 3 read as a prediction about readership, which is checkable against publication figures for the decades after 1820, and which the text does not attempt to support from data.’ A satisfactory answer numbers premises; an excellent one identifies which premise the author never defends.
depth.summary: An adverse reading is a specification of what a text would have to be. Treat each one as an argument with premises, hidden criteria and, often, a falsifiable prediction — and treat oddities in the transcription as evidence about the transcriber rather than about the author.

lessons.title: The reply that changes the terms: Shelley’s ‘A Defence of Poetry’
lessons.explanation: The most instructive replies do not deny the opponent’s premises; they show that the premises presuppose something the opponent has not accounted for. Shelley’s ‘A Defence of Poetry’, printed as the final item in the Project Gutenberg collection A Defence of Poetry and Other Essays, answers the position Peacock had taken by redefining the word in dispute. Poetry, in this essay, is not verse: ‘Poetry, in a general sense, may be defined to be “the expression of the imagination”’. Once that definition is in place, the argument about whether versifiers are useful to a scientific age has changed its subject, because imagination is what the scientific age is using. Shelley divides the mental operations explicitly: ‘Reason is the enumeration of quantities already known; imagination is the perception of the value of those quantities, both separately and as a whole’, and he adds the subordination that does the argumentative work — ‘Reason is to the imagination as the instrument to the agent, as the body to the spirit, as the shadow to the substance.’ The reply to utilitarianism is then direct: ‘The great instrument of moral good is the imagination’, and a society with abundant knowledge and no imaginative faculty is diagnosed as one whose ‘calculations have outrun conception’. His most quoted sentence is also his most unguarded: ‘Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world’ [1][2].
lessons.example: Read the reply as a sequence of moves and then decide which moves are sound. Move one, re-definition: ‘poetry’ is enlarged from metrical composition to imaginative expression, which makes Peacock’s evidence — the diminishing audience for verse — a fact about one medium rather than about poetry. Move two, re-description of the dispute: the question is no longer whether poetry is useful but what usefulness presupposes, and Shelley’s answer is that the valuation of any quantity is an imaginative act. Move three, concession: ‘We have more moral, political and historical wisdom, than we know how to reduce into practice’, which grants Peacock’s point about accumulating knowledge and then relocates it, since the failure is not knowledge but the faculty that would apply it, expressed in the phrase ‘We want the creative faculty to imagine that which we know’. Move four, assertion: the final paragraph’s ‘Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world’. The last move is the weakest as argument, and the reason is worth stating precisely. The intervening passage accumulates metaphors — poets as hierophants, mirrors, words, trumpets — and a cadence of parallel clauses; the claim about legislation is the peak of a rhetorical ascent rather than the conclusion of a demonstration. Two further facts about the text should be recorded in any citation: the edition I fetched prints the essay without a date note, and it marks several of the volume’s other pieces as written in one year and published in another, so the essay’s dating should be sought elsewhere rather than inferred from this edition. A fair assessment therefore separates the reply — which is a real answer, because it exposes an unexamined premise about value — from the closing flourish, which asks the reader to be moved rather than convinced. Distinguishing those two functions is a transferable skill and it is exactly what the capstone in lesson 70 requires [1][2].
lessons.question: What is the strongest part of Shelley’s reply to Peacock?
lessons.answer: The argument that reason’s operations presuppose an imaginative act of valuing, which converts Peacock’s contrast between useful knowledge and ornamental poetry into a relation of dependence
lessons.distractor: The final sentence about unacknowledged legislators, since it states the social importance of poets in a form that is easy to remember
lessons.correction: Memorability is not argument, and the closing sentence is preceded by eight metaphors and parallel clauses, which is the form of a peroration rather than of a proof. The load-bearing part of the essay is the reason-and-imagination distinction, because it engages Peacock’s premise about what is useful instead of merely denying that poetry is useless.

depth.definitions: Utility is usefulness, often measured by contribution to practical ends; the utilitarianism of Shelley’s moment treats value as a function of such contribution. Imagination, in this essay, is the faculty that perceives value and composes new wholes; reason is the faculty that enumerates and analyses what is already known. Peroration is the closing movement of a speech or essay, often designed to move rather than to prove. Re-definition is a move that changes a key term’s extension. Prerequisites: lesson 67 on adverse cases, and lesson 58 on review, scholarship and appreciation.
depth.mechanism: Re-definition does two things at once: it enlarges the class of things defended and it makes the opponent’s examples look partial. Its cost is that the dispute can become verbal, a risk Coleridge names when he remarks that controversy is often excited by ‘the disputants attaching each a different meaning to the same word’. The mechanism to extract from Shelley is therefore double-edged. Where the two writers use ‘poetry’ in different senses, the disagreement is partly about a word; where they agree that knowledge must be valued to be used, the disagreement is substantive and Shelley has the argument. A reader who cannot tell the two apart will either dismiss the essay as rhetoric or accept it as proof.
depth.secondExample: Test the same method on a reply in an earlier lesson: Lamb’s prose paraphrase of Shakespeare against the verse, where the question is what a change of medium preserves. There, the reply to ‘prose is enough’ is not that prose is bad but a demonstration that something has been lost, and the demonstration is a comparison rather than a re-definition. The two replies together give a small taxonomy: repair the vocabulary, or repair the evidence. An essay that confuses the two — arguing about definitions while claiming to have settled facts — is the commonest failure of undergraduate writing on criticism, and the diagnostic is to ask which of the two operations each paragraph is performing.
depth.mistake: The characteristic error is to treat Shelley’s essay as the correct answer to Peacock, as if a question of value could be closed by one eloquent document. Diagnose it by asking what Shelley conceded and what the peroration asserts without argument; a reader who cannot answer both has adopted the essay rather than assessed it. The opposite error, treating the essay as pure rhetoric, misses the genuine argument about valuation, which survives the peroration’s inflation.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: write 200 words assessing one sentence from the Defence as argument, one as rhetoric, and one as both, quoting each exactly and naming the edition. Model response, self-reviewed: ‘Argument: “Reason is the enumeration of quantities already known; imagination is the perception of the value of those quantities”, which is a premise with consequences and can be contested by anyone who thinks valuation is a form of calculation. Rhetoric: “Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world”, which compresses a complex claim into an image and offers no evidence of legislative effect. Both: “We want the creative faculty to imagine that which we know”, which states a diagnosis and does so in a phrase that would not survive being unpacked into literal terms.’ A satisfactory answer sorts sentences; an excellent one shows why a sentence can belong to two categories.
depth.summary: A strong reply identifies the premise it does not share and then shows what the opponent’s position presupposes. Separating argument from peroration keeps the analysis honest, because the rhetorical peak of an essay is often the part that carries least evidential weight.
