lessons.title: Arguing about method: Wordsworth’s Preface and Coleridge’s equivocation
lessons.explanation: Disagreement is easier to argue about when the two positions are printed and can be quoted, and this lesson’s pair is a model case: a poet’s manifesto and a poet-critic’s examination of it. In the Preface to the second edition of Lyrical Ballads as printed in Project Gutenberg’s 1800 volume, Wordsworth describes his experiment as one of ‘fitting to metrical arrangement a selection of the real language of men in a state of vivid sensation’, says that his principal object was ‘to make the incidents of common life interesting by tracing in them, truly though not ostentatiously, the primary laws of our nature’, and explains that ‘Low and rustic life was generally chosen because in that situation the essential passions of the heart find a better soil in which they can attain their maturity’. Later he summarises his practice: he has ‘chosen subjects from common life’ and ‘endeavoured to bring my language near to the real language of men’. He also offers a definition: ‘Poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity’. In Biographia Literaria, chapter XVII, Coleridge sets out to examine what he calls the tenets peculiar to Mr. Wordsworth, summarising his own chapter as follows: ‘Rustic life (above all, low and rustic life) especially unfavourable to the formation of a human diction--The best parts of language the product of philosophers, not of clowns or shepherds--Poetry essentially ideal and generic--The language of Milton as much the language of real life, yea, incomparably more so than that of the cottager.’ His central complaint is a logical one: ‘I object, in the very first instance, to an equivocation in the use of the word “real.”’ [1][2]
lessons.example: Two lessons come out of this pair, and the second one is about evidence discipline. The first is Coleridge’s method of locating the disagreement. He refuses to argue about whether Wordsworth’s poems are good, and instead restates the propositions he means to oppose, quoting them: ‘a selection of the real language of men’, and then what he calls the sentence against which ‘exclusively’ his opposition is directed: ‘Between the language of prose and that of metrical composition, there neither is, nor can be, any essential difference’. Having isolated the claim, he defines the real question in a way that makes it answerable: ‘whether there are not modes of expression, a construction, and an order of sentences, which are in their fit and natural place in a serious prose composition, but would be disproportionate and heterogeneous in metrical poetry’. The equivocation charge follows: ‘real’ slides between what a peasant actually says, what is common to all users of the language, and what is true to feeling, and Coleridge proposes a replacement term, ‘For “real” therefore, we must substitute ordinary, or lingua communis.’ The second lesson is subtler and it concerns your own practice as a reader. Coleridge quotes Wordsworth as writing ‘I have proposed to myself to imitate, and, as far as is possible, to adopt the very language of men’. In the 1800 Preface text I fetched, those words do not appear; the corresponding sentence is the one quoted in the explanation — ‘endeavoured to bring my language near to the real language of men’. The reason is almost certainly that the Preface was revised in later editions and Coleridge quotes the later wording, which I could not fetch to confirm. So the correct conclusion is not ‘Coleridge misquotes’, nor ‘Coleridge quotes accurately’, but: an edition a disputant uses may not be the edition you are reading, and before alleging misquotation you must establish which version the disputant had in front of him. That is the same discipline as the collation in lesson 61, applied to prose about poems [1][2].
lessons.question: Coleridge’s first objection to Wordsworth’s Preface is that the word ‘real’ is used equivocally. Why does that objection have to precede the others?
lessons.answer: Because the claim being opposed depends on the word: if ‘real language’ can mean common language, actual rustic speech, or language true to feeling, then the supporting evidence differs for each sense and the argument cannot be assessed until the sense is fixed
lessons.distractor: Because equivocation is a formal fallacy, and any argument containing a fallacy is invalid from the start and needs no further examination
lessons.correction: The reason is about the shape of the dispute, not about formal validity. A term used in more than one sense makes the evidence underdetermined, since the same example can confirm one reading and refute another; fixing the sense is what makes the subsequent objections testable. Calling the argument invalid and stopping would leave Coleridge’s own substitute term unexamined, and his chapter goes on to make substantive claims about diction that deserve assessment in their own right.

depth.definitions: An equivocation is the use of one word in two senses within an argument; the ‘real question’ is a formulation that puts a dispute in testable form. Poetic diction is the vocabulary and usage deemed appropriate to verse. Lingua communis, in Coleridge’s phrase, is language common to all users rather than peculiar to a class. Concession is a point granted to an opponent. Prerequisites: lesson 67 on adverse cases, lesson 68 on re-definition, and lesson 61 on witnesses and editions.
depth.mechanism: Coleridge’s chapter performs four operations in order: it restates the opponent’s propositions in the opponent’s own words, isolates the one proposition he opposes, reformulates the question so that it can be answered by examples, and then supplies counter-examples from the poems. The order matters, because an objection to a position requires a fixed target; an essay that objects without isolating the claim will be answered by the observation that the author said something else elsewhere. The limitation is that restating an opponent’s words is itself an interpretive act, as the quotation question in this lesson shows; Coleridge’s target is a text he does not name by edition, so a reader cannot always tell which version of the Preface the target is.
depth.secondExample: Apply the four operations to Wordsworth’s own defence of metre, which is where the two writers come closest. Wordsworth argues that metre is justified because the pleasure it gives qualifies the emotion, and Coleridge argues from the origin of metre as a ‘spontaneous effort’ that holds passion in check. Both accounts make metre a moderator of feeling, so the disagreement at this point is about mechanism rather than about value, and it can be stated as a question with two candidate answers. Writing that comparison forces precision of a kind that writing about taste does not, and it is the same operation as Coleridge’s restatement, performed on two texts rather than one.
depth.mistake: The standing misconception is that a dispute about method is a dispute about quality, so that siding with Coleridge means thinking less of Wordsworth’s poems. Diagnose it by separating the claim from the poems: Coleridge’s chapter concedes much of Wordsworth’s practice while denying his theory of diction, and a reader who cannot state which of the two is being assessed has not yet entered the argument. The second misconception is the mirror image, treating the Preface as a description of the poems; a manifesto is evidence about intention, not about the texts.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: choose one proposition from the Preface, quote it with the edition you used, and write 250 words that (a) restates it in your own words, (b) names one poem or passage that would test it, and (c) reports whether your test supports, complicates or refutes it. Model response, self-reviewed: ‘Proposition quoted: “Poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity”. Restated: composition begins from a recalled emotion that the writer then contemplates. Test: the ‘Tintern Abbey’ lines on returning to the Wye, where the poem narrates the recollection it describes. Result: complicates rather than confirms, because the poem’s account of tranquillity is an argument the poem makes about itself, so the test is circular unless I find evidence outside the poem — a letter or a draft — about how it was written.’ A satisfactory answer quotes with a source; an excellent one notices when its own test is circular.
depth.summary: To argue about method, isolate the claim, fix the senses of its key words, and separate a doctrine from the works it claims to explain. Then check the edition, because a quotation you cannot locate may belong to a version you have not read.

readings.title: [1] William Wordsworth, Preface to Lyrical Ballads, in Lyrical Ballads, with Other Poems, 1800, Volume 1, Project Gutenberg
readings.note: Read the Preface in full, particularly the paragraphs on the choice of common life, on bringing language near to ‘the real language of men’, and on poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings. This is the 1800 version, which matters for the quotation question discussed in the lesson.

readings.title: [2] Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Biographia Literaria, chapter XVII, Project Gutenberg
readings.note: Read from the chapter summary that begins ‘Examination of the tenets peculiar to Mr. Wordsworth’ through the objection about the word ‘real’ and the restatement of the true question. Chapter XIV’s definition of a poem and its remark about disputants attaching different meanings to the same word are worth reading in the same sitting. Public domain in the USA.

visual.title: Four operations of a disputant: how Coleridge argues with a preface
visual.description: A flow diagram of chapter XVII’s method, from restating the opponent’s propositions to isolating one claim, reformulating the question, and testing it against examples.
steps: Operation 1 — restate: Coleridge quotes Wordsworth’s phrasing, including ‘a selection of the real language of men’
Operation 2 — isolate: he names the single proposition he opposes, that prose and metrical composition differ in no essential respect
Operation 3 — reformulate: the real question becomes whether certain constructions are proper in prose but disproportionate in metre
Operation 4 — test: counter-examples are sought in the poems themselves, and the substitute term ‘ordinary, or lingua communis’ is proposed

Edition check: the words Coleridge quotes as Wordsworth’s (‘adopt the very language of men’) do not appear in the 1800 Preface fetched here, so the version quoted must be established before alleging misquotation
Transfer rule: fix the target, fix the senses, then object — in that order

lessons.title: Capstone: your own comparative case, with its strongest objection and a falsification test
lessons.explanation: The level ends with production rather than reception: you will build a comparative argument about two poems you have read closely, state the strongest objection to it, answer the objection, and specify what evidence would make you withdraw the thesis. Everything in lessons 61 to 69 feeds this task. The reading for the exercise is a paragraph of literary criticism rather than a poem, because criticism is where comparisons are usually made and where they usually go wrong. In chapter XIV of Biographia Literaria, Coleridge offers a definition — ‘A poem is that species of composition, which is opposed to works of science, by proposing for its immediate object pleasure, not truth’ — and then a warning that applies to every comparison you will write: ‘Controversy is not seldom excited in consequence of the disputants attaching each a different meaning to the same word’. Earlier in the same chapter he had described the effect of the Lyrical Ballads plan as procuring ‘that willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith’. Read together, these three sentences give the capstone its shape: define your terms before you compare (61, 65), isolate the respect in which the works are being compared (66), represent the opposing case at its strongest (67), show which of your opponent’s premises you accept and which you dispute (68), and check the edition of everything you quote (69) [1]
lessons.example: Here is the task in full, with the rubric exposed. Choose two poems from this level: any pair from Blake’s ‘London’, Milton’s Book I opening, Donne’s ‘A Valediction: forbidding mourning’, Hopkins’s ‘God’s Grandeur’ or ‘The Windhover’, Keats’s ‘Ode on a Grecian Urn’, Shelley’s ‘Ozymandias’ or Smith’s. Write 800 to 1,000 words with the following five components, each of which is separately scored. Component one, a thesis stating a claim about how the two poems differ in one named respect, not a claim that both poems are about X. Component two, at least two quotations per poem, each attributed to a named witness with the edition identified, and each verified against the text you actually consulted. Component three, the strongest objection to your thesis, stated in a form its own defender would accept, which usually means granting the descriptive facts and disputing the inference. Component four, your answer to the objection, which must concede something. Component five, a falsification clause: the specific textual or historical evidence that would make you abandon the thesis. A model thesis, on the pair used in lesson 66: ‘Smith’s sonnet can name London and Shelley’s cannot, because Shelley’s scene is enclosed in a traveller’s report; the difference is structural rather than temperamental.’ The strongest objection: ‘The frame is a convention of Romantic orientalism and carries no argumentative weight, so the difference in naming is a difference of opportunity, not of design.’ The answer concedes the convention and replies that a convention can be used, pointing to the moved quotation mark between the 1818 and 1819 texts, which shows the poet revising the boundary of the reported speech. The falsification clause: if a draft or a letter showed the traveller’s frame added late, after the moral was written, the structural claim would weaken considerably. Note what the rubric forces: every component can fail on its own, and the falsification clause is not decoration — an argument that cannot imagine its own refutation is, on this rubric, incomplete [1][2][3].
lessons.question: Which sentence satisfies the falsification requirement of the capstone rubric?
lessons.answer: If a draft or letter showed that the traveller’s frame was added after the moral, the claim that the frame does the argumentative work would be weakened and I would revise it
lessons.distractor: My claim is supported by two quotations from each poem, so no further evidence could overturn it
lessons.correction: Evidence that supports a thesis cannot also be the condition of its defeat, and no thesis is beyond revision. A falsification clause names a specific, imaginable piece of evidence and says what would follow from finding it, which is what makes the argument honest and testable. The correct answer does both, and it also says what would change rather than simply asserting confidence.

depth.definitions: A thesis is a contestable claim about the text; an objection is the strongest reason against it; a reply concedes something and answers anyway; a falsification clause specifies evidence that would defeat the thesis. Attribution means naming the witness and edition for every quotation. A rubric is a scoring description of what success looks like. Prerequisites: the whole level, especially lessons 61 on witnesses, 65 on whole-poem argument, 66 on grounds of comparison, 67 on adverse readings and 69 on disputation.
depth.mechanism: The five components work because each one closes a route of escape. The named-respect thesis prevents the essay from retreating into shared themes; the attributed quotations prevent unattributable paraphrase; the objection requirement forces engagement with the best counter-case rather than a straw one; the concession prevents the reply from being a denial; and the falsification clause converts the essay from an assertion into an argument with a stated failure condition. The limitation is that no rubric guarantees quality; it can be satisfied by an incompetent argument that names its respects and its evidence. That is why the level closes with the reminder that completing a rubric is not the same as being right, and why the parent course does not treat these quizzes as evidence of professional competence.
depth.secondExample: Run the rubric against a weaker version of the same task to see what it excludes. A weaker essay might claim: ‘Both Shelley and Smith use the image of a ruined statue to show that power does not last.’ It has a topic, no named respect of difference, no attributed witnesses, an objection that would be ‘some might disagree’, a reply that repeats the thesis louder, and a falsification clause that says the evidence is plentiful. Revising only the first component — naming the respect of difference as the presence or absence of a frame — changes the whole essay, because it tells the writer what evidence to gather. This is why the order of the rubric is not arbitrary, and why component one is worth revising first.
depth.mistake: The most common failure is a thesis that cannot be false, such as ‘Both poems explore the transience of earthly power with rich imagery’. Diagnose it by asking what evidence would refute it; if nothing would, it is a description and not a thesis. The second failure is quoting from memory without checking the text — the specific danger this subject’s rules exist to prevent, since a plausible-looking line that does not appear in any edition is indistinguishable, in an essay, from a fabricated one.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: complete the five-component essay as described, using the model thesis, objection, reply and falsification clause as structural guides rather than as content to reproduce. Model response, self-reviewed against the rubric: ‘Thesis names one respect: the frame. Quotations: two from each poem, each with edition and witness identified, both checked against the text I fetched. Objection: stated in a form a defender of the opposing view would accept, and it is granted the convention. Reply: concedes the convention’s existence and argues from the moved quotation mark between the 1818 and 1819 printings. Falsification: a draft showing the frame added late, with the consequence stated. Self-review: my weakest component is the reply, because the moved quotation mark is evidence about punctuation and not yet about intention; I have said so rather than pretending otherwise.’
depth.summary: An interpretation is finished when it can state its own strongest objection and the evidence that would end it. That standard is stricter than being persuasive, and it is the standard the whole course has been building toward since the first defensible claim.

visual.title: Five components of a defensible comparative essay
visual.description: A rubric diagram connecting each required component to the failure it prevents, drawn as a chain from thesis to falsification clause.
steps: Component 1 — thesis naming one respect of difference, which prevents a comparison that only lists shared themes
Component 2 — two attributed and verified quotations per poem, which prevents paraphrase from memory
Component 3 — the strongest objection, stated as its defender would state it, which prevents the straw opponent
Component 4 — a reply that concedes something, which prevents the reply that merely repeats the thesis
Component 5 — a falsification clause naming evidence and the consequence of finding it, which converts assertion into argument
Self-review column completed honestly, including which component is weakest and why

questions.prompt: A student compares Shelley’s and Smith’s ‘Ozymandias’ sonnets and writes that both poems show pride punished by time, which proves that Romantic poets shared a single view of empire. A tutor asks for the ground of comparison. What is missing?
questions.answer: A named respect in which the poems differ, since shared themes predict nothing and cannot be tested by evidence from either poem
questions.distractor: A third poem by a different author, since comparison requires at least three texts to establish a general claim
questions.correction: The number of texts is not the problem; the missing element is a variable. Because the two sonnets share occasion, form and subject, the comparison becomes informative only when one respect of difference is isolated, such as the presence of a traveller’s frame in Shelley against direct narration and a named modern city in Smith. Shared themes are what makes the pair comparable, not what the comparison demonstrates.

questions.prompt: A seminar attacks Peacock’s essay by observing that poetry is still being written and read two centuries later. Which assessment of that rejoinder is most accurate?
questions.answer: It refutes one part of Peacock’s case, his prediction about reception, while leaving his premise about the measurement of value and his criterion of usefulness untouched
questions.distractor: It refutes the whole essay, since a prediction that fails destroys the argument that contained it
questions.correction: Peacock’s essay contains claims of different kinds, and they do not all stand or fall together. Falsifying the forecast addresses one of them; the prior premise that value is a function of contribution to useful knowledge, and the criterion by which poetry is judged ornamental, remain to be argued about, which is why lesson 67 insists that an adverse case be disaggregated before it is answered.

questions.prompt: A reader says Shelley’s essay answers Peacock because it is more eloquent and ends with the memorable sentence about unacknowledged legislators. Which correction is most useful?
questions.answer: Eloquence is not the measure: the substantive answer lies in the argument that reason presupposes the imagination’s act of valuing, while the closing sentence is a peroration that moves rather than proves
questions.distractor: The essay does not answer Peacock at all, since Shelley never mentions him by name and never quotes his essay
questions.correction: Not naming an opponent is not the same as not answering him: Shelley’s redefinition of poetry as imaginative expression and his claim that valuation precedes utility engage the position directly. But the strength is located in those arguments, not in the rhetorical climax, and a reader who cannot say which sentence does which job has adopted the essay instead of assessing it.

questions.prompt: An essay states that Wordsworth and Coleridge disagreed because Coleridge preferred Milton’s diction to rustic speech, and therefore Coleridge thought Wordsworth’s poems bad. Which criticism is best supported by the texts?
questions.answer: The second inference overreaches: Coleridge restates and grants much of Wordsworth’s practice, and his chapter opposes a theory of diction rather than condemning the poems
questions.distractor: The first statement is false because Coleridge never mentions Milton in the chapter
questions.correction: Coleridge’s own chapter summary makes the Milton comparison explicitly, calling the language of Milton more the language of real life than that of the cottager, so the first statement stands. What fails is the step from a disagreement about diction to a verdict on the poems, which the chapter does not support and which confuses a claim about method with a judgement of quality.

questions.prompt: A student’s capstone thesis reads: ‘Both poems use vivid imagery to explore how human beings confront mortality, and each does so in its own way.’ A reviewer returns it. What is the reviewer’s strongest ground?
questions.answer: The thesis cannot be false, names no respect in which the poems differ, and offers no evidence that would count against it, so it describes rather than argues
questions.distractor: The thesis is too long and uses the word ‘vivid’, which is a subjective term inappropriate to academic writing
questions.correction: Length and word choice are minor; the failure is structural. A thesis must be contestable and must direct the reader to evidence, and this one accommodates any two poems on any theme, so no quotation could confirm or disconfirm it. The repair is to name a single respect of difference and then collect evidence that bears on it, which is what lesson 70’s rubric requires.

questions.prompt: Two nineteenth-century reprints of a lyric silently normalise the contractions, capitals and hyphens of the original printing, while the wording of the clauses is unchanged. A student concludes that the reprints are textually identical to the original and can be quoted interchangeably. Assess the conclusion, and say what kind of personification evidence the normalisation may have removed.
questions.answer: The conclusion covers only wording: the contractions cue elision in performance and the capitals mark personified agents, so the reprints may quote clause for clause while still altering how the poem is read aloud and who counts as an agent in it
questions.distractor: The conclusion is correct because textual identity is determined by wording, and punctuation, capitalisation and contractions are matters of typography rather than text
questions.correction: Wording is one witness layer among several. In the poem studied in lesson 61, the plate’s apostrophes instruct the reader to elide, and its capitals mark ‘Man’, ‘Church’ and ‘Harlot’ as agents; a reprint that removes both leaves the clauses identical and the reading different. The student is right about wording and wrong to extend that to identity, and the useful essay would grade the differences as elisional, personifying and inert.

questions.prompt: A poem suspends its main verb across five lines while the line-ends coincide with no clause boundary, and elsewhere places an object at a line-end with its agent and verb at the start of the next line. A reader claims both devices create hesitation. Which assessment best distinguishes the two? Assess the reader’s claim, name the syntactic feature that distinguishes the two devices, and state what a defender of the single-device view would have to show.
questions.answer: The suspension delays a required element and is measurable as a syntactic fact, whereas the inverted placement moves emphasis within a clause the reader can already parse, so only the first forces the reader to hold a structure open
questions.distractor: Both devices are the same phenomenon, since any mismatch between line and syntax produces the same effect of hesitation
questions.correction: The two are distinguishable in principle and in the text. A five-line suspension withholds a constituent the sentence cannot do without, so the reader’s parse is incomplete at every pause; putting an object before its subject and verb reorganises a structure that becomes complete within two lines. Treating them as one device is the error that makes prosodic claims unfalsifiable, since no arrangement of lines could then count as evidence against the claim.

questions.prompt: An essay argues that a poet’s figurative language is ‘rich and suggestive’, illustrating the claim with four images from four different poems. A second reader objects that the essay describes rather than argues. What would the second reader require of the essay, and what would the first need to abandon? State precisely what the second reader would require the first essay to produce, and name the inference about imagery that the first essay would have to abandon in order to meet it.
questions.answer: A mapping of at least one figure’s parts onto the parts of the claim it carries, together with a statement of where the mapping is inexact; the first essay would have to abandon the inference that quantity of imagery indicates quality
questions.distractor: A statement of the poet’s intentions, since description becomes argument once the poet’s design has been established from letters or prefaces
questions.correction: Intentions are evidence about intention, not a substitute for an argument about the text. The requested operation is structural: name the vehicle’s parts, assign them to the tenor, and say where the correspondence strains, as with the compasses whose fixed foot is mechanical at the moment the poem needs fidelity to be chosen. Quantity of imagery measures nothing, and the second reader’s demand is a demand for a testable claim.

questions.prompt: A student scans a poem by syllables, reports that the metre is irregular, and then claims the poet wrote free verse before free verse existed. The poem’s author published a preface describing feet of one to four syllables with one principal stress each. What does the preface change about the analysis? Explain what the preface changes about the analysis, and separate that question from the separate question whether the prefix’s claims about the rhythm’s novelty can themselves be tested.
questions.answer: It supplies the unit of measurement, so the analysis must count stresses per line and may legitimately find a regular pattern that a syllable count cannot detect
questions.distractor: It proves the poet’s metrical system was successful, since a poet who theorises his own rhythm must have understood it correctly
questions.correction: The preface changes the unit of measurement, not the verdict on success. Counting stresses may reveal four- and five-stress lines where syllables vary, which defeats the free-verse claim; but the preface is a producer’s account, and its claims about the rhythm’s naturalness and novelty are open to challenge by later scholarship, which is a separate question from how the lines scan.

questions.prompt: Two witnesses of a poem agree in the punctuation of a disputed final couplet but disagree in three earlier places, including one exclamation mark that changes an address into an exclamation. A student argues that the agreement about the couplet settles the question of who speaks the last two lines. How should that inference be qualified?
questions.answer: Agreement between two witnesses is evidence that the reading was transmitted, not that it was intended, and the punctuation itself places the last two lines outside the quoted speech rather than assigning them to a speaker
questions.distractor: The inference is sound, because any reading shared by two independent witnesses must reproduce what the author wrote
questions.correction: Two witnesses to the same printed tradition are not two independent origins, especially when the later one may derive from the earlier volume. What the agreement supports is the state of the transmitted text, which is precisely what makes the crux a crux: in both witnesses the closing quotation mark falls before the final two lines, so no speaker is assigned and the question must be argued on structural evidence, with the limitation stated.

questions.prompt: Two sonnets were written on the same occasion, in the same form, on the same subject, and one encloses its scene inside a traveller’s report while the other narrates directly and closes by naming the poet’s own city. A critic claims the structural difference is merely a difference of technique and has no bearing on the poems’ arguments. Build the best answer to that critique.
questions.answer: The frame restricts what the poem can report, so the absence of a named modern city follows from the narrative choice rather than from the poet’s indifference, and the difference is therefore argumentative in its consequences
questions.distractor: The critique is right, because technique and argument are separate departments of a poem and only the argument can be assessed
questions.correction: Technique and argument are separable in analysis but not in consequence. A reported scene cannot contain what the reporter did not witness, so the poem’s silence about its own nation is entailed by its structure, and the moral has nowhere to land except on sand. The critic’s premise is that effects must be stated in the poem’s themes rather than traced through its architecture, and the answer shows what that premise costs. Evidence for the answer includes the poet’s own revision of the boundary of the reported speech between the two early printings.

questions.prompt: A critic argues that a genre has become obsolete because the knowledge it once carried is now carried by other disciplines, and predicts that its audience will dwindle to nothing. A second critic attacks one poem for relying on conventions that no longer move a reader, calling its diction harsh and its rhymes uncertain. Compare the two adverse cases in terms of what would be needed to answer each.
questions.answer: The first requires an empirical answer to a forecast about reception plus an argument about the premise that value tracks contribution to knowledge, while the second requires contesting a criterion of sincerity and then arguing about its application to one poem
questions.distractor: Both require the same answer, namely that each work is widely admired, since reception is the only available evidence about literary value
questions.correction: The two cases fail differently. A forecast can be checked against the record, which makes part of the first objection answerable by evidence, though the unstated premise about usefulness must still be argued. A criterion of sincerity cannot be checked against the record; it must be contested or applied differently, and the second critic’s own concessions about beauty in the poem’s sentiments show how a criterion-based attack is conducted. Answering both with applause meets neither case.

questions.prompt: An essay replies to a critic by arguing that the critic uses a key word in two senses, and then treats the dispute as settled. A second essay replies by showing what the critic’s own position presupposes. Which reply is stronger, and what does the weaker one leave undone? Decide which reply is stronger, and state what the weaker of the two leaves unassessed once the terminology has been repaired.
questions.answer: The second is stronger because it engages the substance of the position; the first fixes a term but leaves the underlying claim unassessed, and a dispute can be partly verbal while still containing a real difference
questions.distractor: The first is stronger because establishing an equivocation refutes the argument outright, and nothing remains to be answered
questions.correction: Naming an equivocation is a necessary repair, not a refutation, and Coleridge’s warning that disputants often attach different meanings to the same word cuts both ways. Once the sense of the term is fixed, the substantive question remains: whether valuation is prior to utility, or whether certain constructions belong to verse rather than prose. The second essay does that work; the first stops at the vocabulary and would have to continue.

questions.prompt: You are asked to assess a dispute between a poet’s preface and a critic’s examination of that preface. The critic quotes a sentence from the preface that does not appear in the edition you have fetched, and the critic states the question at issue as whether verse admits constructions that would be alien in serious prose. What should your essay do, and in what order?
questions.answer: Establish which version of the preface each text quotes, then separate the doctrine from the poems, then assess whether the restated question is answerable by examples and whether the critic’s substitute term improves the formulation
questions.distractor: Conclude that the critic misquotes and therefore misrepresents, since a quotation that cannot be located in the only edition available must be erroneous
questions.correction: An unlocatable quotation is a problem about editions before it is a problem about honesty: the preface was revised, and the words may belong to a version not fetched, which is why the first step is bibliographic. Only then can the doctrine be tested against the poems, and only then can the reformulated question be evaluated. Declaring misrepresentation on the strength of one edition inverts the order and converts a scholarly question into an accusation.

questions.prompt: A student’s comparative essay names a respect of difference, quotes two lines from each poem with editions identified, states an objection in the opponent’s own terms, replies with a concession, and adds a falsification clause. A reviewer says the essay is now defensible. Which residue of risk remains, and how should the essay disclose it?
questions.answer: The rubric can be satisfied by an argument whose quotations, though verified, do not bear on the named respect of difference, so the essay must say explicitly which of its quotations supports the thesis and which merely illustrates it
questions.distractor: None remains, because a thesis, attributed evidence, an objection, a reply and a falsification clause together constitute a complete argument
questions.correction: Completeness of form is not soundness of support. A quotation can be accurate and irrelevant, which is the commonest way a well-structured essay fails; the remedy is to state, quotation by quotation, what claim it supports, and to name the component of the argument that is weakest. The capstone’s own model response does this by conceding that its reply rests on punctuation evidence and not yet on intention.

questions.prompt: A teacher selects three poems from this level to teach the difference between a variant, a transcription artefact and an editorial normalisation. For each category, name the evidence a student would need in order to place a given difference correctly, and say what follows about the strength of any interpretive claim built on it.
questions.answer: A variant needs at least two witnesses compared, an artefact needs a source that is more authoritative than the copy in hand, and a normalisation needs the edition’s stated policy; claims built on artefacts are the weakest because the difference may not exist in any document the author saw
questions.distractor: All three categories require the same evidence, namely the earliest available printing, which by definition preserves what the author wrote
questions.correction: The three cases rest on different comparisons. A variant is established by comparing witnesses and stating which reading each carries; an artefact is a difference that disappears when a more reliable copy is consulted, as with a probable copying error in a transcription; a normalisation is a documented decision by an editor, stated in a preface or a note. Earliest-wins collapses them and also fails on its own terms, since the earliest printing may be a transcription of a lost manuscript.

questions.prompt: A seminar asks you to defend the proposition that a poem’s meaning includes the state of its text. Using two of this level’s poems, set out the strongest version of that proposition, the best objection to it, and the evidence that would settle the dispute in each case. Set out the strongest version of the proposition, the best objection to it, and the evidence that would settle the dispute in each of your two chosen cases.
questions.answer: The proposition holds where a textual difference alters an inferable structure such as who speaks or who acts, and fails where the difference is inert; in each poem the settling evidence would be a witness showing the other reading in the poet’s own hand or in the printing he oversaw
questions.distractor: The proposition is true for all poems, since every mark on a page is part of the work and no difference between witnesses can ever be dismissed as inert
questions.correction: Universalising the proposition destroys its usefulness, because a claim that everything matters cannot be tested by any evidence. The defensible version is local: a variant matters when it changes what can be inferred, as when a verb becomes a noun and the agent of perception changes, and it does not matter when it alters only spelling. The objection is that meaning should be identified with an authorial text rather than with a set of documents, and the evidence that settles each local case is a witness closer to the author — a manuscript or an overseen printing — which is exactly the evidence collation seeks and rarely finds.
